title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: the Chandogya Upanishad, a text of the Sama Veda, follows a chain from the ground under your feet to the high chant, link by link

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda: verses from the Rig Veda set to melody, opening with come, Agni, to the feast.

Orange juice in a carton. Before that, oranges in a crate. Before that, a tree; before that, rain and soil. Every glass at breakfast sits at the end of a chain nobody follows back. One old text follows a chain like that, link by link, from the ground up, but it isn't tracing breakfast. It's tracing a song. The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Sama Veda, and right at its start it asks what the very best part of everything is, and keeps going until it reaches the chant itself.
screen: `A GLASS OF JUICE, A CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `ONE TEXT TRACES A SONG.` → `THE CHAIN THAT ENDS IN A CHANT.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya opens with the udgitha, the high chant, the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up. It says, in paraphrase: let a person meditate on the syllable Om as the udgitha, for the chant begins with Om. Then comes the chain. The essence of all beings is the earth. The essence of the earth is water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human being. Of the human being, speech. Of speech, the Rig Veda's verses. Of the Rig Veda, the saman, the melody. And of the saman, the udgitha, which is Om. Walk it slowly: the ground, the rain in it, what grows from the rain, the people fed by it, their voices, the best words a voice can say, those words sung, and at the heart of the singing, one syllable. Each link is the rasa, the juice, the essence, of the one before. So in this picture a song isn't a pleasant extra laid on top of the words. It's what the words are reaching toward. And Om sits at the end of a line that starts with dirt. The Upanishad doesn't float the sacred syllable above ordinary things. It grows it from soil, water and food, through a body and a voice. Every Om, in this reading, has a field behind it.
screen: `THE UDGITHA: THE HIGH CHANT.` · `EARTH, WATER, PLANTS, PEOPLE, SPEECH.` · `VERSE, THEN MELODY, THEN OM.` · `EVERY OM HAS A FIELD BEHIND IT.`

segments.voice: Feel the ground under you, then the water in you, then the last thing you ate, grown somewhere, then yourself here, a person, walking the chain link by link. Let a quiet sound come on the out-breath, a hum, a word, or Om if you use it, and rest in the quiet after it before going around again. If you pray, rest in prayer at the end.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the melody is the essence of the verse, and the high chant's heart is Om. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. From soil to song, one link at a time. Day twelve seventy-five, done.

screen: `DAY 1275 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG.`

what a scholar hears: rasa, juice or essence: each link (earth, water, plants, person, speech, ṛc, sāman, udgītha) is the rasa of the one before (Chandogya 1.1.2).
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

chat.says: Why does that Upanishad start a chain with dirt and end with Om?
options: Each link is the essence of the one before, so Om grows from earth, through us.
It's saying Om is only dirt, so the sacred syllable has no special worth.
It ranks things, so people and speech matter less than plants and water.
chat.meaning: Chandogya 1.1 runs earth, water, plants, person, speech, verse, melody, udgitha: each the essence of the one before, with Om at the end.

notes: Paraphrase of Chandogya 1.1.1–2: confirm the order of the chain (beings → earth → water → plants → person → speech → ṛc → sāman → udgītha) and the gloss of rasa as 'essence'.
Udgītha described as 'the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up' is a simplification of the udgātṛ's portion of the chant; confirm.
Max Müller's 1879 Upanishads translation is public domain but is not on the validator's list, so all English is paraphrase.
